stream-a-13-pride-prejudice.text: “If I can but see one of my daughters happily settled at Netherfield,” said Mrs. Bennet
to her husband, “and all the others equally well married, I shall have nothing to wish
for.”
In a few days Mr. Bingley returned Mr. Bennet’s visit, and sat about ten minutes with
him in his library. He had entertained hopes of being admitted to a sight of the young
ladies, of whose beauty he had heard much; but he saw only the father. The ladies were
somewhat more fortunate, for they had the advantage of ascertaining, from an upper
window, that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.
An invitation to dinner was soon afterwards despatched; and already had Mrs. Bennet
planned the courses that were to do credit to her housekeeping, when an answer arrived
which deferred it all. Mr. Bingley was obliged to be in town the following day, and
consequently unable to accept the honour of their invitation, etc. Mrs. Bennet was quite
disconcerted. She could not imagine what business he could have in town so soon after
his arrival in Hertfordshire; and she began to fear that he might always be flying about
from one place to another, and never settled at Netherfield as he ought to be. Lady
Lucas quieted her fears a little by starting the idea of his being gone to London only
to get a large party for the ball; and a report soon followed that Mr. Bingley was to
bring twelve ladies and seven gentlemen with him to the assembly. The girls grieved over
such a number of ladies; but were comforted the day before the ball by hearing that,
instead of twelve, he had brought only six with him from London, his five sisters and a
cousin. And when the party entered the assembly-room, it consisted of only five
altogether: Mr. Bingley, his two sisters, the husband of the eldest, and another young
man.
Mr. Bingley was good-looking and gentlemanlike: he had a pleasant countenance, and easy,
unaffected manners. His sisters were fine women, with an air of decided fashion. His
brother-in-law, Mr. Hurst, merely looked the gentleman; but his friend Mr. Darcy soon
drew the attention of the room by his fine, tall person, handsome features, noble mien,
and the report, which was in general circulation within five minutes after his entrance,
of his having ten thousand a year. The gentlemen pronounced him to be a fine figure of a
man, the ladies declared he was much handsomer than Mr. Bingley, and he was looked at
with great admiration for about half the evening, till his manners gave a disgust which
turned the tide of his popularity; for he was discovered to be proud, to be above his
company, and above being pleased; and not all his large estate in Derbyshire could save
him from having a most forbidding, disagreeable countenance, and being unworthy to be
compared with his friend.
Mr. Bingley had soon made himself acquainted with all the principal people in the room:
he was lively and unreserved, danced every dance, was angry that the ball closed so
early, and talked of giving one himself at Netherfield. Such amiable qualities must
speak for themselves. What a contrast between him and his friend! Mr. Darcy danced only
once with Mrs. Hurst and once with Miss Bingley, declined being introduced to any other
lady, and spent the rest of the evening in walking about the room, speaking occasionally
to one of his own party. His character was decided. He was the proudest, most
disagreeable man in the world, and everybody hoped that he would never come there again.
Amongst the most violent against him was Mrs. Bennet, whose dislike of his general
behaviour was sharpened into particular resentment by his having slighted one of her
daughters.
Elizabeth Bennet had been obliged, by the scarcity of gentlemen, to sit down for two
dances; and during part of that time, Mr. Darcy had been standing near enough for her to
overhear a conversation between him and Mr. Bingley, who came from the dance for a few
minutes to press his friend to join it.
“Come, Darcy,” said he, “I must have you dance. I hate to see you standing about by
yourself in this stupid manner. You had much better dance.”
“I certainly shall not. You know how I detest it, unless I am particularly acquainted
with my partner. At such an assembly as this, it would be insupportable. Your sisters
are engaged, and there is not another woman in the room whom it would not be a
punishment to me to stand up with.”
“I would not be so fastidious as you are,” cried Bingley, “for a kingdom! Upon my
honour, I never met with so many pleasant girls in my life as I have this evening; and
there are several of them, you see, uncommonly pretty.”
“You are dancing with the only handsome girl in the room,” said Mr. Darcy, looking at
the eldest Miss Bennet.
“Oh, she is the most beautiful creature I ever beheld! But there is one of her sisters
sitting down just behind you, who is very pretty, and I dare say very agreeable. Do let
me ask my partner to introduce you.”
“Which do you mean?” and turning round, he looked for a moment at Elizabeth, till,
catching her eye, he withdrew his own, and coldly said, “She is tolerable: but not
handsome enough to tempt me; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to
young ladies who are slighted by other men. You had better return to your partner and
enjoy her smiles, for you are wasting your time with me.”
Mr. Bingley followed his advice. Mr. Darcy walked off; and Elizabeth remained with no
very cordial feelings towards him. She told the story, however, with great spirit among
her friends; for she had a lively, playful disposition, which delighted in anything
ridiculous.

stream-a-14-mill-on-floss.text: On Wednesday, the day before the aunts and uncles were coming, there were such various
and suggestive scents, as of plumcakes in the oven and jellies in the hot state, mingled
with the aroma of gravy, that it was impossible to feel altogether gloomy: there was
hope in the air. Tom and Maggie made several inroads into the kitchen, and, like other
marauders, were induced to keep aloof for a time only by being allowed to carry away a
sufficient load of booty.
“Tom,” said Maggie, as they sat on the boughs of the elder-tree, eating their jam-puffs,
“shall you run away to-morrow?”
“No,” said Tom, slowly, when he had finished his puff, and was eying the third, which
was to be divided between them,—“no, I sha’n’t.”
“Why, Tom? Because Lucy’s coming?”
“No,” said Tom, opening his pocket-knife and holding it over the puff, with his head on
one side in a dubitative manner. (It was a difficult problem to divide that very
irregular polygon into two equal parts.) “What do I care about Lucy? She’s only a
girl,—she can’t play at bandy.”
“Is it the tipsy-cake, then?” said Maggie, exerting her hypothetic powers, while she
leaned forward toward Tom with her eyes fixed on the hovering knife.
“No, you silly, that’ll be good the day after. It’s the pudden. I know what the pudden’s
to be,—apricot roll-up—O my buttons!”
With this interjection, the knife descended on the puff, and it was in two, but the
result was not satisfactory to Tom, for he still eyed the halves doubtfully. At last he
said,—
“Shut your eyes, Maggie.”
“What for?”
“You never mind what for. Shut ’em when I tell you.”
Maggie obeyed.
“Now, which’ll you have, Maggie,—right hand or left?”
“I’ll have that with the jam run out,” said Maggie, keeping her eyes shut to please Tom.
“Why, you don’t like that, you silly. You may have it if it comes to you fair, but I
sha’n’t give it you without. Right or left,—you choose, now. Ha-a-a!” said Tom, in a
tone of exasperation, as Maggie peeped. “You keep your eyes shut, now, else you sha’n’t
have any.”
Maggie’s power of sacrifice did not extend so far; indeed, I fear she cared less that
Tom should enjoy the utmost possible amount of puff, than that he should be pleased with
her for giving him the best bit. So she shut her eyes quite close, till Tom told her to
“say which,” and then she said, “Left hand.”
“You’ve got it,” said Tom, in rather a bitter tone.
“What! the bit with the jam run out?”
“No; here, take it,” said Tom, firmly, handing, decidedly the best piece to Maggie.
“Oh, please, Tom, have it; I don’t mind—I like the other; please take this.”
“No, I sha’n’t,” said Tom, almost crossly, beginning on his own inferior piece.
Maggie, thinking it was no use to contend further, began too, and ate up her half puff
with considerable relish as well as rapidity. But Tom had finished first, and had to
look on while Maggie ate her last morsel or two, feeling in himself a capacity for more.
Maggie didn’t know Tom was looking at her; she was seesawing on the elder-bough, lost to
almost everything but a vague sense of jam and idleness.
“Oh, you greedy thing!” said Tom, when she had swallowed the last morsel. He was
conscious of having acted very fairly, and thought she ought to have considered this,
and made up to him for it. He would have refused a bit of hers beforehand, but one is
naturally at a different point of view before and after one’s own share of puff is
swallowed.
Maggie turned quite pale. “Oh, Tom, why didn’t you ask me?”
“I wasn’t going to ask you for a bit, you greedy. You might have thought of it without,
when you knew I gave you the best bit.”
“But I wanted you to have it; you know I did,” said Maggie, in an injured tone.
“Yes, but I wasn’t going to do what wasn’t fair, like Spouncer. He always takes the best
bit, if you don’t punch him for it; and if you choose the best with your eyes shut, he
changes his hands. But if I go halves, I’ll go ’em fair; only I wouldn’t be a greedy.”
With this cutting innuendo, Tom jumped down from his bough, and threw a stone with a
“hoigh!” as a friendly attention to Yap, who had also been looking on while the eatables
vanished, with an agitation of his ears and feelings which could hardly have been
without bitterness. Yet the excellent dog accepted Tom’s attention with as much alacrity
as if he had been treated quite generously.
But Maggie, gifted with that superior power of misery which distinguishes the human
being, and places him at a proud distance from the most melancholy chimpanzee, sat still
on her bough, and gave herself up to the keen sense of unmerited reproach. She would
have given the world not to have eaten all her puff, and to have saved some of it for
Tom. Not but that the puff was very nice, for Maggie’s palate was not at all obtuse, but
she would have gone without it many times over, sooner than Tom should call her greedy
and be cross with her. And he had said he wouldn’t have it, and she ate it without
thinking; how could she help it? The tears flowed so plentifully that Maggie saw nothing
around her for the next ten minutes; but by that time resentment began to give way to
the desire of reconciliation, and she jumped from her bough to look for Tom.

Lines 31 to 34 keep the two apart for Mr Darcy too: 'his manners gave a disgust' is one fault and his 'disagreeable countenance' another.

questionLines: When Mr Darcy first walked in, the room thought very well of him. Read lines 26 to 30. Why?

options.value: Because he danced with lots of different ladies.
options.tagDescription: Assigns a detail the text gives to one character or thing to another, or the right attribute at the wrong value.
options.tagChildHint: Check who or what each detail belongs to in the text.
options.execution: Dancing every dance is Mr Bingley at line 37, carried across to Mr Darcy, who dances twice. In the window, line 27 answers the stem: 'drew the attention of the room by his fine'.

options.value: Because he spoke kindly to everyone he was introduced to.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Speaking kindly is nowhere; line 40 has him decline being introduced to anyone.

options.value: Because he was the tallest man in the room.
options.tagDescription: Chooses always/never/impossible options when the text is measured.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'The tallest man in the room' is the absolute version of line 27's 'fine, tall person'.

options.value: Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.
Because he owned a large estate in Derbyshire.
options.tagDescription: Answers from a detail in the wrong part of the passage.
options.tagChildHint: Something from another part of the passage does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The Derbyshire estate is line 33, and it appears only when the room has turned against him. In the window, line 27 answers the stem: 'drew the attention of the room by his fine'.

cards.hint: What had everybody heard about him within five minutes?
cards.walkScript: Start at line 27, with 'his fine, tall person'. Line 29 adds 'ten thousand a year'. So his looks and his money won the room. The estate is named later.

questionLines: Halfway through the evening, people changed their minds about Mr Darcy. Read lines 30 to 35. What changed them?

options.value: They found out that he was not really rich after all.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Nothing says the money was doubted; line 33 still calls the estate large.

options.value: They decided he was less good-looking than Mr Bingley.
options.tagDescription: The child picks a cause that happens LATER in the passage than the effect being asked about. The two events are both real and both about the same people, so the option reads well; only the order rules it out.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Lines 34 and 35 do have the room find his face forbidding and him unworthy to be compared with Mr Bingley. That verdict comes after his manners turned the tide at lines 31 and 32, so the child gives the result of the change as its cause.

options.value: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.
He was angry, complaining that the ball had ended far too early.
options.tagDescription: Assigns a detail the text gives to one character or thing to another, or the right attribute at the wrong value.
options.tagChildHint: Check who or what each detail belongs to in the text.
options.execution: Line 37 gives this to Mr Bingley, who 'was angry that the ball closed so early', and the child carries it across to Mr Darcy. Lines 31 to 33 give what changed the room: 'his manners gave a disgust', as he was found 'to be proud, to be above his company'.

options.value: Everybody disliked him from the moment he walked in.
options.tagDescription: Chooses always/never/impossible options when the text is measured.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'From the moment he walked in' overstates: line 30 has him admired for half the evening.

cards.hint: Find the word 'till' in line 31 and read on from there.
cards.walkScript: Find 'till' in line 31. 'His manners gave a disgust' and turned the tide. So his behaviour changed the room's mind. His money and looks come earlier.

questionLines: Read lines 36 to 41. The writer suddenly says: 'What a contrast between him and his friend!' Why is that sentence put there?

options.value: To tell the reader that the two men had fallen out.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A quarrel is nowhere in the passage; the two are together again at lines 49 and 51.

options.value: To show that Mr Bingley was cross about something.
options.tagDescription: The option states something that is true inside the cited window and answers a different question from the one asked. The child has located the right lines and taken the wrong element out of them. A named sub-route is the WRONG SPEAKER: the material is inside the window but belongs to the other party in an exchange — one child's answer offered where the other child's instruction was asked for. The cure is the same in both cases, so the sub-route shares this hint.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: The anger at line 37 is inside the window and is Mr Bingley's, about the ball closing early — the wrong element of a line the item does use.

options.value: To show that the writer likes Mr Darcy the better of the two.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A preference is supplied for the writer, who states the contrast and takes no side in it.

options.value: To make the reader notice how differently the two men were behaving.
To show that the two men were really rather alike.
options.tagDescription: The child reads a word that names a relationship between two things (contrast, unless, however, instead of) as its opposite, usually as plain 'and' or 'the same as'. The result is an option that keeps every fact but reverses how the facts sit together.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: 'Contrast' is read as its opposite. The sentence says the two men are unlike, and this answers that they are alike.

cards.hint: Read the sentence before it and the sentence after it.
cards.walkScript: Look at each side, lines 36 to 41. Mr Bingley 'danced every dance'; Mr Darcy walks about alone. So you see how differently they behave. Nothing says they fell out.

questionLines: Read lines 39 to 41. How many dances did Mr Darcy dance, and who did he dance with?

options.value: Every dance of the evening.
options.tagDescription: Assigns a detail the text gives to one character or thing to another, or the right attribute at the wrong value.
options.tagChildHint: Check who or what each detail belongs to in the text.
options.execution: Every dance belongs to Mr Bingley: line 37 says he 'danced every dance'. The child carries it across to Mr Darcy, who at lines 39 and 40 'danced only once with Mrs. Hurst and once with Miss Bingley'.

options.value: Two: one with Mrs Hurst and one with Miss Bingley.
Two: once with Elizabeth Bennet and once with Miss Bingley.
options.tagDescription: Matches an option on gist when it differs from the text, or from the key, by a single word or detail.
options.tagChildHint: An answer can look almost like the text. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: One name changed: Elizabeth Bennet for Mrs Hurst. Line 40 has Mr Darcy dance 'once with Mrs. Hurst and once with Miss Bingley'. Elizabeth sits down for two dances at lines 47 and 48, and Mr Darcy turns her down at lines 66 and 67.

options.value: None at all.
options.tagDescription: Chooses always/never/impossible options when the text is measured.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'None at all' is the absolute version of 'danced only once... and once' at lines 39 and 40.

options.value: Three: with Mrs Hurst, Miss Bingley and Miss Bennet.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A third dance with Miss Bennet is supplied; she dances with Mr Bingley at line 63 and never with him.

cards.hint: Count how many times the word 'once' appears.
cards.walkScript: The sentence about Mr Darcy starts at line 39. He danced once with Mrs Hurst and once with Miss Bingley. That is two dances, and every dance belongs to Mr Bingley.

questionLines: Read lines 41 to 43. The writer says: 'His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world.' What do these short, sure sentences do?

options.value: They prove that Mr Darcy really was the worst man alive.
options.tagDescription: Chooses always/never/impossible options when the text is measured.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: 'Really was the worst man alive' takes the room's verdict as the writer's own finding.

options.value: They show that the writer had run out of things to say about him.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A motive is supplied for the writer; the shortness is doing the room's certainty, not his.

options.value: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.
They show that Mr Darcy had at last made up his mind about something.
options.tagDescription: The child applies the word's commonest everyday sense in a context that does not support it. The sense chosen is a real sense of the same word; it is simply the one that arrives first, and the sentence around the word is what should have displaced it. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items: it occurs wherever a word's sense is load-bearing, including on technique stems.
options.tagChildHint: Words can have more than one meaning. Check that the meaning you used fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: Takes 'his character was decided' as Mr Darcy deciding something. NOTE REPAIRED 2026-08-16 (delivery 52): 'decided' meaning MADE A DECISION is the sense that arrives first, not 'the other sense' — the passage's sense, settled and no longer open to question, is the rarer one. The error is a dominant sense displacing a rarer one. Tag grandfathered; the note is not.

options.value: They tell us that Mr Darcy said nothing to anybody all evening.
options.tagDescription: Chooses an option the passage explicitly denies, rather than one it merely fails to support. Distinguished from a plausible option the passage never states: here the passage states the contrary. Negation-dropped loses a WORD; this loses a CLAIM, and the option may share no wording with the line that refutes it.
options.tagChildHint: The passage says something different. Go back and find it.
options.execution: Lines 41 and 42 have Mr Darcy speaking occasionally to one of his own party, so the passage states the contrary. The child takes his coldness to mean total silence and misses what the short, sure sentences do.

cards.hint: Notice how certain these short sentences are. Then ask what they are based on.
cards.walkScript: Look at line 42: 'His character was decided'. Nobody is named as deciding it. So the room's hasty view sounds like a fact. It comes after one night.

questionLines: Mrs Bennet was one of the people most against Mr Darcy. Read lines 44 to 46. What made her dislike of him stronger?

options.value: He had been rude about one of her daughters.
He would not let anyone introduce him to her.
options.tagDescription: Answers from a detail in the wrong part of the passage.
options.tagChildHint: Something from another part of the passage does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Declining to be introduced is line 40, and it is to any other LADY, not to Mrs Bennet in particular. Lines 45 and 46 give her own reason: he had slighted one of her daughters.

options.value: He had told Mr Bennet that he did not like the neighbourhood.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Mr Bennet is not at the ball at all in this passage, and no such remark is made.

options.value: Mr Bingley had chosen to dance with her eldest daughter.
options.tagDescription: Attributes the right event to the wrong cause or character.
options.tagChildHint: Ask who did this, or what caused it, in the text. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: The cause is moved to Mr Bingley's dancing with the eldest daughter at lines 60 and 61; lines 45 and 46 name the slight as the reason.

options.value: He was the proudest man in the world, and she hated proud people.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: The child takes line 42's 'the proudest ... man in the world' and adds a general reason, a dislike of proud people, that the passage never gives Mrs Bennet. Lines 45 and 46 give her own reason: he had slighted one of her daughters.

cards.hint: Read lines 44 to 46. Find the words that say what turned her dislike into something stronger.
cards.walkScript: Read lines 44 to 46. He had 'slighted one of her daughters'. Slighted means treated as nothing. So the sting is her own child.

questionLines: Elizabeth had to sit down for two dances. Read lines 47 to 48. Why?

options.value: She did not feel like dancing that evening.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A wish not to dance is supplied; line 47 says she was OBLIGED to sit down.

options.value: Mr Darcy was standing near enough for her to hear him.
options.tagDescription: The option states something that is true inside the cited window and answers a different question from the one asked. The child has located the right lines and taken the wrong element out of them. A named sub-route is the WRONG SPEAKER: the material is inside the window but belongs to the other party in an exchange — one child's answer offered where the other child's instruction was asked for. The cure is the same in both cases, so the sub-route shares this hint.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True of lines 48 and 49: Mr Darcy 'had been standing near enough for her to overhear a conversation' with Mr Bingley. That is what happened while she sat, not why she sat. Line 47 gives the reason: she was 'obliged, by the scarcity of gentlemen, to sit down'.

options.value: She wanted to listen to Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley talking.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A motive is supplied; line 48 has the overhearing happen because he stood near enough, not because she arranged it.

options.value: There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.
Her eldest sister was dancing with Mr Bingley.
options.tagDescription: Answers from a detail in the wrong part of the passage.
options.tagChildHint: Something from another part of the passage does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: Her eldest sister dancing with Mr Bingley is line 60, true, and not the reason line 47 gives.

cards.hint: Find the word in line 47 that says she had no choice. What forced her?
cards.walkScript: Line 47 holds the reason. She was 'obliged, by the scarcity of gentlemen, to sit down'. A scarcity means too few men for the ladies. Mr Darcy's words come later.

questionLines: Elizabeth hears Mr Darcy's words herself. A friend does not tell her later. Read lines 47 to 50. Why is that a good choice?

options.value: It shows that Elizabeth enjoyed listening in on other people.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A taste for listening in is supplied; line 48 has him standing near enough for her to overhear.

options.value: It shows that the room had almost emptied by then.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: An empty room is not stated; line 49 has Mr Bingley coming from the dance, so it is in progress.

options.value: The reader hears the unkind words at the very moment Elizabeth does.
Mr Bingley had planned for her to hear his kind words about her.
options.tagDescription: Attributes the right event to the wrong cause or character.
options.tagChildHint: Ask who did this, or what caused it, in the text. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Elizabeth does overhear Mr Bingley's kind words about her at lines 62 and 63. But nothing says he planned it: line 50 has him come to press his friend to dance, and line 48 gives the real cause, Mr Darcy standing near enough for her to overhear.

options.value: It shows that Mr Darcy was speaking loudly to the whole room.
options.tagDescription: Chooses an option the passage explicitly denies, rather than one it merely fails to support. Distinguished from a plausible option the passage never states: here the passage states the contrary. Negation-dropped loses a WORD; this loses a CLAIM, and the option may share no wording with the line that refutes it.
options.tagChildHint: The passage says something different. Go back and find it.
options.execution: Lines 48 and 49 have Elizabeth overhear a conversation between Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley, because Mr Darcy was standing near her. The child turns overhearing into Mr Darcy speaking loudly to everyone, which those lines contradict.

cards.hint: Imagine a friend passing the words on to her later instead. What would the reader miss?
cards.walkScript: Line 48 puts him 'near enough for her to overhear'. So the words come in his voice. You hear them as Elizabeth does.

questionLines: Read lines 51 and 52. Mr Bingley says to his friend: 'I hate to see you standing about by yourself in this stupid manner.' What is Mr Bingley trying to do?

options.value: Tell his friend off for being rude about the ladies.
options.tagDescription: Answers from a detail in the wrong part of the passage.
options.tagChildHint: Something from another part of the passage does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The rudeness about the ladies is at lines 55 and 56, in Mr Darcy's reply, after this speech. Mr Bingley's aim is at line 51: 'I must have you dance.'

options.value: Get his friend to join the dancing.
Ask his friend to leave the ball and go home.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Going home is nowhere; the speech asks him to move onto the floor, not off it.

options.value: Make his friend feel sorry for the ladies who have no partner.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Pity for partnerless ladies is supplied; the speech is about his friend and no one else.

cards.hint: What does he ask for at the start, and again at the end?
cards.walkScript: Read the speech, lines 51 and 52. It opens 'I must have you dance', ends 'You had much better dance'. So he wants his friend dancing. 'Stupid' describes the standing about.

questionLines: Read lines 53 to 56. Mr Darcy says: 'Your sisters are engaged.' What does 'engaged' mean here?

options.value: They have promised to marry somebody.
options.tagDescription: The child applies the word's commonest everyday sense in a context that does not support it. The sense chosen is a real sense of the same word; it is simply the one that arrives first, and the sentence around the word is what should have displaced it. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items: it occurs wherever a word's sense is load-bearing, including on technique stems.
options.tagChildHint: Words can have more than one meaning. Check that the meaning you used fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: Promised in marriage is the sense a child meets first, and a ballroom full of unmarried people supports it.

options.value: They are busy and cannot be spoken to.
options.tagDescription: The child chooses another genuine sense of the same word, neither the commonest one nor the one the passage fixes. The option is defensible in isolation and is ruled out only by the surrounding text, so the child gets no signal that anything is wrong. This holds only where the surrounding text fixes the sense decisively. Where it does not, the option is a defensible second answer and the item is faulty rather than hard. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: Busy and not to be interrupted sits right beside the passage sense and is not it: line 54 is about who is free to DANCE.

options.value: They are standing and talking with Mr Bingley.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Standing and talking with Mr Bingley is not stated; he is dancing at line 60.

options.value: They do not want to dance with Mr Darcy.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A wish not to dance with him is supplied; line 54 says nothing about what the sisters want.

options.value: They have already promised their dances to other partners.

cards.hint: He is making a list of who is free to dance. Where do the sisters go on that list?
cards.walkScript: Look at the speech, lines 53 to 56. He lists who he might dance with, crossing the sisters off. So their dances are already promised. Marriage is the better-known sense.

questionLines: Read lines 57 to 59. Mr Bingley cries: 'I would not be so fastidious as you are.' What does 'fastidious' mean here?

options.value: Very hard to please.
Very quick and in a hurry.
options.tagDescription: The meaning the child chooses belongs to a DIFFERENT WORD that the target resembles in form, or to a morpheme she has met in other words. She has not chosen among the target's senses at all — she has misidentified the word. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items.
options.tagChildHint: This word looks like one you know. Read it letter by letter and check it is the same word.
options.execution: The child sees 'fast' at the start of 'fastidious' and gives the meaning of that different word. Line 57 has Mr Bingley say he would not be so fastidious as Mr Darcy, which is about being hard to please, not about speed.

options.value: Very shy with people you do not know.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Shyness is not in the passage; Mr Darcy's objection at lines 53 and 54 is to the company, not to himself.

options.value: Very tidy and neat.
options.tagDescription: The child chooses another genuine sense of the same word, neither the commonest one nor the one the passage fixes. The option is defensible in isolation and is ruled out only by the surrounding text, so the child gets no signal that anything is wrong. This holds only where the surrounding text fixes the sense decisively. Where it does not, the option is a defensible second answer and the item is faulty rather than hard. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: Tidy and neat is a real everyday use of the word and nothing in these lines is about order.

options.value: Very rude to other people.
options.tagDescription: Picks a meaning that belongs to no sense of the word and to no word it resembles in form.
options.tagChildHint: This word never means that. Put your answer in its place. Read the sentence again.
options.execution: Rude is no meaning of 'fastidious' and belongs to no word it looks like. The child reaches for what Mr Darcy is like elsewhere in the passage, cold at line 66, instead of what the word names.

cards.hint: The two friends are looking at the very same room. How are they different about it?
cards.walkScript: Lines 57 to 59 give the sense. Bingley met many 'pleasant girls'; Darcy sees none worth a dance. So fastidious means very hard to please. Shy and tidy do not fit here.

questionLines: Read lines 65 to 67. Mr Darcy says Elizabeth 'is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me'. What does 'tolerable' mean here?

options.value: Kind, and easy to get along with.
options.tagDescription: Picks a meaning that belongs to no sense of the word and to no word it resembles in form.
options.tagChildHint: This word never means that. Put your answer in its place. Read the sentence again.
options.execution: Kind and easy to get along with is no meaning of 'tolerable'. The child guesses a word about temperament, where line 66 uses it about how Elizabeth looks: only just good enough.

options.value: Good at putting up with things without complaining.
options.tagDescription: The meaning the child chooses belongs to a DIFFERENT WORD that the target resembles in form, or to a morpheme she has met in other words. She has not chosen among the target's senses at all — she has misidentified the word. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items.
options.tagChildHint: This word looks like one you know. Read it letter by letter and check it is the same word.
options.execution: Putting up with things without complaining is the meaning of 'tolerant', a different word the target resembles in form. The child has misidentified the word; line 66 uses 'tolerable' about how Elizabeth looks.

options.value: Only just good enough to look at.
Very good-looking, so he is paying her a compliment.
options.tagDescription: Chooses an option the passage explicitly denies, rather than one it merely fails to support. Distinguished from a plausible option the passage never states: here the passage states the contrary. Negation-dropped loses a WORD; this loses a CLAIM, and the option may share no wording with the line that refutes it.
options.tagChildHint: The passage says something different. Go back and find it.
options.execution: Lines 66 and 67 say at once that she is 'not handsome enough to tempt me', which states the contrary of very good-looking. The child reads 'tolerable' as praise and does not read on to the rest of the sentence.

options.value: Too proud to dance with anybody.
options.tagDescription: Assigns a detail the text gives to one character or thing to another, or the right attribute at the wrong value.
options.tagChildHint: Check who or what each detail belongs to in the text.
options.execution: The pride belongs to Mr Darcy, who at line 32 is found to be proud and above his company. The child moves it onto Elizabeth, whom the word 'tolerable' describes at line 66.

cards.hint: Read the word 'but' that follows. It takes the praise straight back.
cards.walkScript: Read on from 'tolerable' in line 66. It is 'but not handsome enough to tempt me'. So it means only just good enough. Putting up with things belongs to a different word, tolerant.

questionLines: Read lines 70 to 73. Elizabeth 'told the story, however, with great spirit'. What does 'spirit' mean here?

options.value: A ghost.
options.tagDescription: The child applies the word's commonest everyday sense in a context that does not support it. The sense chosen is a real sense of the same word; it is simply the one that arrives first, and the sentence around the word is what should have displaced it. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items: it occurs wherever a word's sense is load-bearing, including on technique stems.
options.tagChildHint: Words can have more than one meaning. Check that the meaning you used fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: A ghost is the sense a child meets first, and nothing in the sentence rules it out until you read on.

options.value: Anger.
options.tagDescription: Chooses an adjacent emotion word rather than the precisely evidenced one.
options.tagChildHint: Find the words in the text that show the feeling. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Anger is an approximation of the feeling: line 70 gives 'no very cordial feelings', and line 71 gives the telling as lively.

options.value: Care and quietness, so that nobody else heard.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Quietness is not stated; line 71 has her telling it 'among her friends'.

options.value: Being lively and cheerful.
Bravery when you are in danger.
options.tagDescription: The child chooses another genuine sense of the same word, neither the commonest one nor the one the passage fixes. The option is defensible in isolation and is ruled out only by the surrounding text, so the child gets no signal that anything is wrong. This holds only where the surrounding text fixes the sense decisively. Where it does not, the option is a defensible second answer and the item is faulty rather than hard. Scoped to the ERROR, not to vocabulary items.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: Bravery in danger is a real second sense of 'spirit' and there is no danger in the line.

cards.hint: Read on past 'spirit'. The rest of the sentence tells you what she was like.
cards.walkScript: Line 71 does not stop at 'spirit'. Read on to line 72: she had 'a lively, playful disposition'. So spirit here means lively and cheerful. A ghost is the other sense.

questionLines: At the end, Elizabeth turns what happened into a story for her friends. Read lines 70 to 73. What does this tell us about her?

options.value: She has completely forgiven Mr Darcy.
options.tagDescription: Picks real-world-plausible options the passage never states, especially motives.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Forgiveness is not stated; line 70 leaves her with 'no very cordial feelings towards him'.

options.value: She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.
She wants her friends to feel sorry for her after how badly she was treated.
options.tagDescription: Attributes a plausible motive the text never supports.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: A wish for sympathy is supplied. Mr Darcy's slight at lines 66 to 68 is real, but lines 71 to 73 say she told the story 'with great spirit' because she 'delighted in anything ridiculous', which is the opposite of asking for pity.

options.value: What Mr Darcy said did not bother her at all.
options.tagDescription: Chooses always/never/impossible options when the text is measured.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
